extracted.intended_audience: researchers and clinicians conducting or interpreting lifestyle/behavior-change obesity intervention trials and systematic reviews
extracted.subtask_short: systematic review of mediators in obesity interventions
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic review protocol and results identifying psychological self-regulation mediators/predictors of weight, physical activity, and dietary outcomes in adult lifestyle obesity interventions, with methods for study selection, data extraction, mediation testing, and quality assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study eligibility — publication date and language
rubrics_metrics.description: Included studies were intervention studies published since 2000 in the English language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to restrict to studies published since 2000 was based on greater external validity of more recent lifestyle intervention research; complete search strategies can be obtained from the authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study eligibility — study design and population
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies had to use experimental designs and refer to clinical or community behavior change interventions with overweight/obese adults (≥18 years old) aiming to reduce overweight/obesity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both randomized and non-randomized experimental designs were considered; participants had to be adults (≥18) and overweight/obese.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study eligibility — definition of 'lifestyle interventions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Lifestyle interventions were defined as interventions that promote change in energy balance-related behaviors (such as diet and physical activity) and self-regulatory factors (such as motivation and self-monitoring) relevant for overweight/obesity treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically in settings involving personal contact between interventionists and participants; no restrictions on format and duration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome timing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: To be eligible, studies should report outcomes assessed at least 6 months after the start of the intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review divides results into short-term (<12 months) and long-term (≥12 months), with 12 months chosen as threshold between weight loss and weight loss maintenance per expert panel guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required outcomes — quantitative measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible studies must include a quantitative assessment of change in weight/BMI, physical activity, or dietary intake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: weight/BMI change (kg, percent, residualized scores), physical activity via self-report or objective (accelerometry/pedometry/attendance), dietary intake via food-frequency or food records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required mediator measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligible studies must include a quantitative assessment of potential mediators of successful behavior change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only mediators representing individual-level self-regulatory processes were considered (skills, motivation, competence, coping mechanisms, beliefs, physical self-perceptions, and eating regulation factors such as disinhibition, restraint, perceived hunger).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded mediator types
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain potential mediators were excluded from consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediators associated with personality factors, social support, and health-related outcomes (psychological distress, quality of life, well-being) were excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an a priori mediator list for inclusion/exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: An a priori list of mediators, based on previous work, was used to decide study inclusion/exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only individual-level self-regulatory processes on that list were eligible; authors can provide the a priori list on request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search strategy and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Comprehensive searches were conducted in specified electronic databases and supplemented by manual cross-referencing and journal hand searches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Databases: PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, Web of Knowledge, SPORTDiscus. Search terms combined population (overweight/obesity), interventions, outcomes (weight/PA/diet), predictors/mediators (psychological/self-regulation), and type of analyses (mediation, correlates, predictors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Study selection process
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles, abstracts, and references were reviewed by two authors to identify studies meeting eligibility; duplicates removed; full texts reviewed and inclusion/exclusion decided by consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two independent reviewers (EVC, MM) carried out screening; discrepancies resolved by consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data extraction standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Data extraction was performed using a form informed by PRISMA and the Cochrane tool and included detailed study characteristics and analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extracted items: study details (authors, year, country, funding), participants (characteristics, recruitment, setting, attrition, compliance, blinding), study design and setting, outcomes, mediators/predictors (in/out list), intervention length and characteristics, psychosocial instruments, statistical analysis including mediation techniques. Authors were contacted for missing data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation testing approaches accepted
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal mediation may be tested using a range of statistical approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approaches mentioned: Baron & Kenny causal steps, MacKinnon/MacKinnon et al. approaches, Preacher & Hayes bootstrap procedures, structural equation modeling (SEM) with bootstrap. Results from formal mediation analyses were reported separately from predictor/correlational analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for inferring mediation in non-formal tests
rubrics_metrics.description: In studies not performing formal mediation tests, results were considered consistent with mediation if two conditions were present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: a) Significant intervention-control differences for a given variable (or pre-post change in non-controlled designs) (path a); and b) association between these changes (in intervention group only) and changes in the outcome (path b). If both present, results deemed consistent with mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study quality assessment — adapted EPHPP tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological quality of included studies was assessed with an adapted Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) Quality Assessment Tool covering 19 items and 8 domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eight domains: 1) study design, 2) blinding, 3) representativeness (selection bias), 4) representativeness (withdrawals/dropouts), 5) confounders, 6) data collection, 7) data analysis, 8) reporting. Each domain classified as Strong (low risk), Moderate, or Low (high risk). Two researchers independently rated domains and overall quality; discrepancies resolved by consensus. Global rating determined from component scores; see Additional file 5 for full scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation-analysis-specific quality checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: For studies employing formal mediation tests, methodological quality was complemented with a mediation-specific checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist (Lubans/Foster/Biddle; adapted by Rhodes & Pfaeffli) includes 11 yes/no questions summed to a global score. High quality = 9–11, moderate = 5–8, low <5. Two authors rated mediation quality; inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa) reported (0.78).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and grouping of mediators
rubrics_metrics.description: To aid interpretation, identified mediators/predictors were grouped into categories based on similarity of definition/operationalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twelve categories formed: Self-regulatory skills use, Processes of change, Coping mechanisms, Self-efficacy/barriers, Autonomous motivation, Controlled motivation, Decisional balance, Outcome expectations/beliefs, Body image/physical self-worth, Cognitive restraint, Eating disinhibition, Perceived hunger. Tables show number of studies, times tested, and percent showing significant effects; mediation-specific results presented separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data synthesis choices for mediation vs prediction studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Only controlled trials were included in synthesis of data from studies formally testing mediation; prediction studies (not formally testing mediation) included both controlled and uncontrolled trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was to strengthen causal inference for mediation analyses while leveraging larger evidence for predictor studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome measurement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and examples for measuring outcomes were specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight measures: calibrated digital scales; weight change expressed as percent from baseline, kilograms, residualized scores, or BMI change. Physical activity: objective assessment (accelerometry, pedometry, attendance) or self-report (Seven-Day Physical Activity Recall, Godin Leisure-Time Exercise Questionnaire). Dietary intake: Food Intake Questionnaire, Three-Day Food Records, Block Food-Frequency Questionnaire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting of mediation analysis power and baseline control
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of mediation analyses included reporting on pilot testing and statistical power, and whether outcomes were controlled for baseline values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors noted none of the studies reported pilot studies for mediation; most did not report power to detect mediation. Only six studies controlled outcomes for baseline values.
